CHAPTER V The Siren's Song

Silas, the old marina watchman, had no trouble confirming their suspicions about the man in the gray sedan. He’d been down to the docks almost every evening for a week, asking questions about the Black Point lighthouse.

"He's a professor, or says he is," Silas reported, polishing a brass cleat until it gleamed. "From the university inland. Says he's studying tidal erosion."

"No doubt he's studying something," was Leo's quiet comment. He and Sam had not talked to the watchman at length before, so he pressed for more details about the strange humming from the lighthouse.

"Heard it three times this week alone, not counting the first time you boys noticed it," the old man said. "Funny thing about the night the fog was thickest."

"What was funny?" Sam asked.

"The light."

"But the lighthouse is decommissioned," Leo exclaimed. "The light hasn't worked in twenty years!"

"Yep. And it didn't work that night, either. Not the big one, anyway. This was a little light, down near the water line. Like someone with a powerful lantern. Saw it from my window, just for a minute or two, right after the humming stopped."

This was a new wrinkle. Leo and Sam looked at each other, confused.

"You've seen this lantern before?" Leo asked.

"Can't say I have. Got no reason to stare at a dead lighthouse, not usually. But I saw it that night. Just a flicker, then it was gone. Then I saw the boat."

"A boat?" Sam demanded. "Whose boat?"

"Don't know. Too dark to see much. Just a little skiff, movin' fast. Headed straight out to sea, not back toward the harbor. Seemed mighty peculiar to me."

"Did you see where it came from?"

"From the rocks at the base of the point, looked like. Me and strange boats in the dark don't mix, boys. I got work to do, but not the kind that gets you tangled in somethin' you can't see."

Leo mulled over the information. "Is this humming always at ten o'clock?"

"No. Sometimes earlier, sometimes later. No rhyme or reason to it."

Leo turned to Sam. "What do you make of that?"

"Nothing," Sam replied. "Not a single thing. You're saying the professor is asking about erosion, a light appears at the water line, and a boat heads out to sea?"

"That's the gist of it. A man who knows tides wouldn't take a skiff out into the open ocean at night, not from Black Point. The currents there are a nightmare."

Sam's face was a mask of concentration. The calm, matter of fact way the watchman added layer upon layer to the puzzle was unnerving. "You mean a real boat, not a ghost ship?" the boy asked, half joking.

"Like I said. A small skiff with an outboard. Heard the motor plain as day, just for a second. It was real enough. Up and down on the swells, then gone."

Leo asked, "Where were you while this was happening?"

"Right here on the pier, gettin' ready to lock up. Scared me some, I'll admit, but not so scared I didn't watch."

A man of true grit, Leo thought. Believed something was wrong, but had the nerve to keep his eyes open. "Mr. Silas, you said the professor was asking questions. Did he ask about the humming?"

"Sure did. Said he'd heard a story about it in town."

Leo considered. "He interested us," he said at last. "He seemed to know a lot about geology, but not much about boats."

Silas's next comment sent Leo's tidy theory into a tailspin. "Oh, he knows boats, all right. I saw him talking to Gus Braddock over at the boatyard. Looked like he was trying to charter Gus's trawler."

Leo looked at Sam, his frustration evident. "Thank you, Mr. Silas," he said glumly. "You've given us a lot to think about!"

The boys watched the old watchman head toward his shack, his heavy boots echoing on the wooden planks. There was no denying what he had heard and seen, only his interpretation of it. Clearly, Leo thought, there was a real boat and a real person at the lighthouse. But what were they actually doing?

"Don't look so defeated," Sam offered. "The professor wanting a boat doesn't mean he isn't our man. Maybe the skiff isn't big enough for whatever he's planning. Maybe he needs a bigger vessel."

"What do you suppose he was doing at the boatyard?" Leo asked.

"Probably just what Silas said. Trying to charter a boat. People do it all the time for fishing trips. No reason the professor wouldn't do the same, to make it look normal."

"We'll stick with our plan," Leo decided. "It's the only real move we have."

By the time the moon began to rise, the boys were in their chosen position, hidden in the dunes that overlooked the path to Black Point. They had a clear view of the winding track, but were themselves invisible behind a wall of sea grass. They had coated themselves in bug spray, but the coastal mosquitoes buzzed around their heads anyway, looking for any spot they had missed. They lay still and watched the empty path, but saw no sign of a gray sedan.

During a long stretch of silence Sam whispered, "You think we missed him? He could have gone out there this afternoon."

"I doubt it. The humming only happens at night. Besides, he'd have to leave his car somewhere, and we checked all the turnoffs on the way here. I don't think he'd want to walk two miles if he didn't have to."

Leo had to admit it made sense. There was no logical reason to park a car any farther away than necessary. The wind picked up, rustling the grass around them. It was almost nine thirty, half an hour before the earliest time they had heard the sound. Leo thought a half hour was more than enough time for someone to get set up inside the lighthouse. That meant they had to wait, to be sure no one slipped past them.

One lone car passed on the distant coastal highway, its headlights sweeping across the dunes, and then the night was silent again.

At ten minutes to ten, Leo gave up. "Either he's not coming tonight, or he got there by sea. Let's get to the overlook."

As they crept through the dunes toward the cliff that overlooked the lighthouse itself, Leo explained his idea to Sam. "That humming has to be mechanical. It's too regular for a natural sound. The only way to make a sound travel that far over water is with some kind of amplifier."

"A giant speaker," Sam agreed. "But why? What's the point?"

That, Leo pointed out, was the million dollar question. "All we can do is watch for that light Silas mentioned. And listen."

"Both ears," Sam corrected.

It was one minute before ten when they reached the edge of the cliff. The old lighthouse stood below them, a dark finger pointing at a sky full of stars. The tide was coming in, and waves crashed against the rocks at its base. By unspoken agreement they moved to a spot sheltered by a rocky outcrop. If a boat approached, they would see its lights long before it reached the point.

"Get ready," Sam whispered. "If that light comes on, I want a picture."

Leo swallowed hard. Despite his certainty that this was all the work of a person, the thought of being so close to the strange event made his skin crawl. The air felt cold and damp. But, he told himself, Sam was right. They had to trust their instincts. "Wait until the humming starts," Leo whispered.

A gull cried out from somewhere behind them, a lonely, mournful sound. The boys held their breath, and in that instant, a low, resonant hum rose from the darkness below.

Leo grabbed Sam's arm. "There it is."
The hum was not loud, but it was pervasive. It seemed to come from all directions at once, a deep thrumming that vibrated in their bones. It grew steadily in volume, a single, pure note that was somehow unsettling.
"Get the camera ready," Leo urged, his voice a low hiss.
Sam was already fumbling with the digital camera, turning the dial to a low-light setting. "I'm on it. Just need the light."
As if on cue, a pale green light bloomed in the lantern room at the very top of the tower. It wasn't the sweeping, powerful beam of a functioning lighthouse. This was a soft, steady glow that pulsed in perfect time with the humming sound. The effect was eerie, transforming the derelict structure into something alien and alive.
"Wow," Sam breathed. He lifted the camera, bracing his elbows on the rock in front of him. The shutter clicked softly, again and again. "Got it. I think."
"What do you make of it?" Leo asked, his eyes fixed on the pulsing green light. "It's not a normal lamp."
"It's a weird color," Sam observed. "Like one of those old computer screens. And it's pulsing. The hum gets a little louder every time the light gets brighter."
This was a new piece of information. Leo listened intently. Sam was right. The sound had a rhythm to it, a slow rise and fall that matched the light. "So they're connected. The sound and the light are coming from the same machine."
"Your giant speaker," Sam said. "Maybe it has a light on it."
"Maybe," Leo agreed, though he was doubtful. "But why? What's the point of the light? It just draws attention to the place."
"Maybe that's the point," Sam countered. "Scare people off. Reinforce the local legends about the place being haunted."
Before Leo could reply, a new sound cut through the night. It was the crunch of tires on a gravel track far below, near the main road. Headlights cut a brief, yellow swath across the dunes before being extinguished. A car door opened, then shut with a solid thud.
The boys flattened themselves against the rock, their hearts pounding.
"That's him," Sam whispered, his voice tight with excitement. "It has to be."
"Shhh."
They waited, straining their ears. For a long minute, there was nothing but the crashing of the waves and the persistent, low hum from the lighthouse. Then, they heard footsteps, slow and steady, coming along the path that led from the road to the base of the tower. A dark figure emerged from the shadows of the dunes, walking with a confident stride. He was just a silhouette against the starlit sand, but he was tall and thin. He carried nothing in his hands.
The figure walked directly to the small, iron-banded door at the base of the lighthouse, produced a key, and let himself inside. The door creaked shut behind him.
Leo and Sam looked at each other in the dim light.
"He went inside," Sam stated the obvious.
"He has a key," Leo added. "He's not breaking in. He belongs there. Or at least, he thinks he does."
"So what do we do now?"
Leo's mind was racing. Their man, almost certainly Mr. Sterling of the gray sedan, was inside the lighthouse with his machine. This was their chance. They might not get another one. The plan they had made was to observe, but the situation had changed.
"We've got to see what's in there," Leo said decisively. "The humming only lasts for about an hour. He'll be in there with it. When he leaves, we go in."
"What if he locks the door?" Sam asked.
"He might not. He might think no one would be crazy enough to come out here at night. And if he does, we'll have to figure something else out. But we can't stay up here."
They waited. The green light continued its slow, rhythmic pulse, and the air vibrated with the unending hum. To the boys, hiding on the cliff, the minutes stretched into an eternity. They watched the stars move slowly across the sky. The tide was still coming in, and the waves against the rocks below sounded angrier, closer.
Finally, after what felt like a lifetime, the green light in the lantern room flickered and died. A moment later, the humming sound ceased. The sudden silence was almost as startling as the noise had been. The only sounds were the wind and the sea.
A few minutes later, the small door at the base of the lighthouse creaked open. The tall, thin silhouette emerged, paused for a second to lock the door behind him, and then began the walk back toward the road.
"He locked it," Sam whispered, his voice full of disappointment. "Now what?"
"Wait," Leo commanded.
They watched as the figure disappeared into the dunes. Soon, they heard a car engine start, and headlights once again swept across the landscape before turning onto the coastal highway and speeding away.
"Okay, let's go," Leo said, already starting to move.
"Go where? He locked the door!"
"There's more than one way into an old building like that," Leo said with a confidence he didn't quite feel. "Especially one that's falling apart. Come on."
They scrambled down a narrow, sandy track that was steeper and more treacherous than it had looked from above. By the time they reached the rocky base of the lighthouse, they were both out of breath. The waves crashed only a few yards away, sending a fine, salty spray into the air.
The iron-banded door was set deep into the stone. Leo grabbed the handle and pulled. It was solid. "Locked tight."
"Told you," Sam said. "Now we're stuck out here for nothing."
"Don't give up yet." Leo began to circle the base of the tower, running his hands over the cold, damp stone. The lower windows were boarded up from the inside, the wood thick and weathered. There seemed to be no way in.
"Leo, maybe we should just go," Sam suggested, casting a nervous glance at the dark, churning water. "The tide's getting pretty high."
"Wait. Look here." Leo pointed to one of the boarded-up windows about five feet off the ground. "This wood looks newer than the rest."
Sam came over. Leo was right. While most of the boards were gray and splintered, two of them were a lighter shade, and the nails holding them in place were shiny, not rusted.
"Pry bar," Sam said instantly. "We should have brought a pry bar."
"We've got the next best thing," Leo said. He rummaged in the small backpack he carried and pulled out a heavy, multi-purpose tool. He unfolded the pliers and then the small, flat-head screwdriver attachment. "It's not much, but maybe it's enough."
He found a small gap between the newer board and the stone casement and wedged the screwdriver head in. He grunted with effort, pushing and wiggling the tool. "I need more leverage."
Sam looked around frantically. "Here." He handed Leo a flat, heavy rock he'd found near the water's edge.
Using the rock as a hammer, Leo carefully tapped the handle of the multi-tool, driving the screwdriver head deeper into the gap. Then, using both hands, he pulled. The wood groaned in protest. A nail screeched as it was slowly pulled from the frame.
"It's working!" Sam whispered excitedly.
It took them ten minutes of grueling work, taking turns prying and pulling, but finally the first board came loose with a splintering crack. The second one was easier. With both boards removed, a dark, rectangular hole gaped in the side of the tower.
"I'll go first," Leo said, his voice echoing slightly in the opening. He tossed his backpack inside, then hoisted himself up and through the narrow window. He landed with a soft thud on a dusty floor. A moment later, Sam followed.
They stood in absolute darkness, the only light a faint gray rectangle from the window they had just entered. The air was thick with the smell of dust, salt, and mildew.
"Flashlight," Sam whispered.
Leo was already digging it out of his pack. A powerful beam cut through the gloom, revealing a large, circular room. The floor was stone, and a spiral staircase made of cast iron dominated the center of the space, winding its way up into the darkness above. The walls were bare stone, weeping with damp. There was nothing else in the room. No furniture, no equipment, nothing.
"It must be upstairs," Leo said, his voice hushed with awe. "At the top."
"That's a lot of stairs," Sam noted nervously.
"We didn't come this far to quit," Leo said, already moving toward the staircase. He tested the first step with his foot. It held firm. "Let's go. And be quiet."
They started the long climb, their footsteps echoing on the metal steps. Leo's flashlight beam danced ahead of them, illuminating the curving stone wall. They passed several landings, each with a boarded-up window and a heavy door leading to what must have once been keeper's rooms. All the doors were shut.
Finally, the staircase ended at a small, round room. This was the lantern room. Large panes of glass, surprisingly clean, circled the entire room, offering a breathtaking view of the dark sea and the distant lights on the mainland.
In the center of the room, just as Leo had predicted, was the source of the mystery. It was not, however, what he had expected.
Mounted on a heavy metal tripod was a strange-looking device. It was a large, parabolic dish, about three feet in diameter, made of a polished, coppery metal. At its focal point, aimed back at the dish, was a thick, green-tinged crystal mounted in a metal housing. Wires snaked from the housing down to a heavy, metal box on the floor. On the box were several dials and a glowing power switch that was now dark.
"What in the world is that?" Sam whispered, walking slowly around the device.
Leo ran his flashlight beam over the apparatus. It looked like something out of a science fiction movie. "I don't know. It's not just a speaker. Look at this dish. And that crystal. It's some kind of emitter."
"For sound?"
"And for light," Leo said, pointing the flashlight at the crystal. "The crystal must be what glows. And the dish... the dish is an amplifier. A resonator. It takes a small sound and focuses it, makes it bigger. And it sends it out in all directions." He tapped the metal box with his knuckle. "And this is the power supply and the controller. He sets the frequency and the pulse here, then turns it on and leaves."
"So it's an experiment?" Sam asked.
"Has to be," Leo said, his mind buzzing with the discovery. "Some kind of acoustics or resonance experiment. That's why he needs a place like this. It's isolated. No one to bother him. No other sounds to interfere with the readings."
Sam pointed to a small, folding camp stool in the corner, next to an open notebook and a pen. "Looks like he sits up here and takes notes while it's running." He walked over and picked up the notebook. "Maybe this will tell us something." He shined his own smaller flashlight on the page. It was filled with columns of numbers and complex-looking equations.
"I can't make sense of any of this," Sam said, flipping through a few pages. "It's all math."
"Let me see." Leo took the notebook. He couldn't understand the equations either, but he recognized some of the symbols from his advanced physics class. And then he saw the notes scrawled in the margins. "Long-range propagation." "Harmonic resonance." "Structural integrity test."
"Structural integrity?" Sam repeated, looking around the room. "You mean of the lighthouse?"
"I think so," Leo said slowly. "He's not just testing sound. He's testing what a specific frequency of sound does to a structure." His eyes widened. "Sam, he could bring this whole place down!"
A floorboard creaked on the stairs below them.
The boys froze, their blood turning to ice. The sound was unmistakable. Someone was coming up the spiral staircase.
Leo clicked off his flashlight. Sam did the same. They were plunged into a disorienting darkness, lit only by the faint starlight coming through the glass. The footsteps grew louder, closer. A heavy, rhythmic tread on the iron stairs.
"Quick, hide!" Sam hissed, diving for the shadows behind the strange machine.
Leo scrambled to the other side of the room, pressing himself into a corner where the curve of the wall offered a small recess. He held his breath, his heart hammering against his ribs. He had been so sure the man had driven away. Had he come back? Had he seen their lights?
The footsteps reached the top of the stairs. A dark figure stepped into the lantern room. It was the same tall, thin man. He didn't turn on a light. He seemed to know his way around perfectly in the dark.
He walked directly to the spot where the notebook had been. He paused. The boys could practically feel his confusion in the tense silence. He had left the notebook open on the stool. Now it was on the floor, where Leo had dropped it.
A powerful beam of light suddenly stabbed through the darkness, sweeping across the room. Leo squeezed his eyes shut as the light passed over him, praying he hadn't been seen. The beam swept past him, then stopped, fixing on Sam's hiding place behind the tripod.
"You can come out now," a calm, low voice said. It was not angry, merely weary. "Both of you."
Slowly, Sam stood up. The flashlight beam stayed on him.
"The other one, too," the man said, without turning.
Defeated, Leo stepped out of his corner. The man swung the flashlight over to him, then back to the window where they had entered. He sighed. It was a sound of profound disappointment.
"You boys have a dangerous amount of curiosity," he said. He clicked on a small battery-powered lantern, filling the room with a steady, white light.
He was older than Leo had expected, probably in his late fifties, with short gray hair and a tired, intelligent face. He wore simple work pants and a dark jacket. It was Mr. Sterling.
"What were you doing?" Leo asked, deciding that a bold question was better than cowering in silence.
The man raised an eyebrow. "I believe that is my question to ask you. This is private property. And you have damaged it to gain entry." He gestured with his flashlight toward the open notebook. "And you have been going through my research."
"Your research is shaking the whole point," Sam said defensively. "People for miles can hear that humming. You're scaring everyone."
"That is an unfortunate but necessary side effect," Mr. Sterling said calmly. "One I am working to minimize." He looked from Leo to Sam, his expression thoughtful. "You are the boys who spoke with Silas Croft, are you not?"
Leo and Sam exchanged a look of surprise. "How did you know?"
"Silas is a talkative man. He mentioned two inquisitive young men were asking about my land offer. I deduced you might take an unhealthy interest in my activities. I did not expect you to be so... resourceful." He glanced at the complex machine on the tripod. "What do you think it is?"
"A resonance emitter," Leo said, his voice gaining confidence. "You're testing the effects of harmonic frequencies on materials. The notes in your book mentioned structural integrity. You're testing the lighthouse."
Mr. Sterling's expression shifted from annoyance to grudging respect. "Very good. You have a future in physics, young man. That is precisely what I am doing. This tower, with its specific stone and iron construction, is the perfect subject for my work on resonant frequencies."
"You want to tear it down," Sam accused.
"Good heavens, no!" Sterling looked genuinely shocked. "The opposite! My work is in historic preservation. I'm developing a system to identify and counteract destructive frequencies. Frequencies caused by wind, by traffic, even by small seismic tremors. Frequencies that can, over decades, weaken and destroy old buildings like this one. By finding the exact resonant frequency of this tower, I can develop a way to neutralize it. To protect it."
This was a completely unexpected turn. Leo's theory of a simple, selfish experiment collapsed.
"But the humming," Leo said, puzzled. "And the light?"
"The hum is the frequency itself, amplified so my sensors can get a clear reading. I am trying to find a way to conduct the tests in the subsonic range, but my equipment is not yet that refined. The light," he said with a sigh, "is a byproduct of the crystal oscillator. I cannot generate the frequency without also exciting the crystal." He looked at them sternly. "My work is important. But it requires isolation. Which is why I made an offer on this land. And why the local ghost stories, which I assure you I did not start, have been a convenient deterrent."
"So you're not trying to scare people away to buy the land cheap?" Sam asked.
"The thought had occurred to me as a beneficial side effect," Mr. Sterling admitted. "But it is not my goal. My goal is to finish my research. Research you have now jeopardized."
He walked over to the window and looked down at the churning sea. "You have seen what I am doing. You are intelligent enough to understand at least the basics of it. What do you intend to do with this information?"
Leo thought for a moment. He looked at the incredible machine, at the pages of complex equations, and at the tired, determined scientist. This wasn't a villain. This was something else entirely.
"We won't tell anyone," Leo said. "On one condition."
Mr. Sterling turned, a flicker of amusement on his face. "You are in no position to make conditions. You are trespassing."
"Your experiment is affecting the town," Leo pressed on. "The humming is disturbing people. If you want to keep your work secret, you have to find a way to stop the noise from traveling so far."
The scientist considered this. He looked back at his machine. "The propagation is wider than I calculated. It's a problem. Perhaps... perhaps I can erect a sonic dampening field around the tower. It would be difficult, but possible. It would require me to recalculate the power output." He looked back at the boys. "If I can guarantee the sound will not leave this point, will you guarantee your silence?"
"We will," Sam said quickly.
"And you will not come back here," Sterling added. "My work is at a delicate stage."
"Agreed," Leo said.
Mr. Sterling nodded, seemingly satisfied. "Very well. Now, I suggest you leave. The way you came. I will repair the window in the morning."

Miller, seeing there was no escape, simply nodded, his gaze fixed on the ground.

"Well," the sheriff said, taking a pair of handcuffs from his belt. "Looks like I'll be having a talk with Mr. Collins tonight after all. The boys walked over to him.

Belsely chewed on this for a long moment, staring at the mine entrance where the apparition had so recently held sway. "Well, I'll be," he said finally. He shook his head, a slow smile spreading across his weathered face. "Dark shadows pullin' a ghost wagon, collectin' invisible dead. And it was just that fella who sells the Frostola bars." He let out a deep, rumbling laugh. "Most curious thing I ever saw. Still is, come to think of it."

Rick and Scotty looked at each other and grinned. The mystery of the Blue Ghost was finally laid to rest, not by ghost hunters, but by a healthy dose of curiosity and a refusal to believe in spirits.

The sheriff listened intently, his expression turning from skepticism to grim understanding. He walked over to the bound Miller and looked him up and down. "Is this true, son? Were you in league with Jethro Collins?"

Miller, seeing there was no escape, simply nodded, his gaze fixed on the ground.

"Well," the sheriff said, taking a pair of handcuffs from his belt. "Looks like I'll be having a talk with Mr. Collins tonight after all. He paused, his mind already shifting from the solved problem to the unanswered questions. "Mr. Belsely, those men, the ones with the cart. They were searching for something, you said. Did you ever see them carry anything away?"

The farmer frowned in thought. "Can't say that I did. Mostly saw them pokin' at the ground. Had little sticks with hoops on the end, now that I think on it."

"Metal detectors," Rick said instantly. "They were looking for the treasure. The one Miller mentioned."

"Treasure?" Belsely's eyes widened. "You mean there's really a treasure?"

"We think so," Scotty confirmed. "That was the whole point of the ghost. To scare people away from the mine and the fields around it so Collins and his men could search undisturbed."

A new light dawned in the farmer's eyes, a look of canny speculation replacing the superstitious fear. "Well, I'll be. All this land around here. Old battlefield, you know. Could be anything. Cannonballs, old rifles, maybe a payroll box the Yankees or our own boys lost. My grandpappy used to tell stories."

Before he could elaborate, the crunch of tires on the gravel road announced the return of the sheriff's car. It pulled to a stop and the portly sheriff climbed out, slamming the door behind him. He looked grim, and he was alone.

"Sheriff?" Rick called out, walking toward him with Scotty at his side. "Did you find Collins?"

The sheriff took off his hat and ran a hand through his thinning hair. "No, I did not. The bird has flown the coop. His office was locked up tight, but I got a warrant from the judge and we went in. Place was cleared out of anything important. Same with the room he was renting. The ice-cream vendor, Miller, must have had a way to signal him that the game was up."

"So he's gone," Scotty said, disappointed.

"Gone for now," the sheriff corrected. "We've put out an alert on him and his car. But a man like Collins, he's slippery. He probably has a hidey-hole somewhere. He was after something, and a man that greedy doesn't give up easy." The sheriff looked at the two boys, his expression softening slightly. "You boys did good work. But I'm telling you now, this is police business. Collins is a cornered man, and that makes him dangerous. I want you to stay clear."

"We understand, Sheriff," Rick said respectfully. But in his mind, a new set of gears was already turning. Collins wasn't just running away, he was running to something. The treasure. "Did you find anything that might tell you where he was going? Or what he was looking for?"

"Not a thing," the sheriff admitted with a sigh. "Just a lot of real-estate papers and a few empty file folders. He wiped the slate clean. We'll get a team out here tomorrow with our own metal detectors, see if we can't find what he was looking for. But this whole area is a state park. It'll be slow going with all the red tape." He put his hat back on. "I'm heading back to town to coordinate the search. You two should get on home. You've had enough excitement for one night."

As the sheriff drove away, Rick turned to Scotty. "He's right about one thing. Collins is a cornered man."

"And he's wrong about another," Scotty added, a familiar glint in his eye. "The excitement isn't over yet."

"Not by a long shot," Rick agreed. "The sheriff will be tied up with official procedures. Collins knows that. He has a head start, and he knows what he's looking for. We don't."

"So what's the plan?"

"We need to know what he knows," Rick said. "And the only person who can tell us that, besides Collins himself, is Miller."

"The Frostola man? You think he'll talk to us?"

"He might," Rick said thoughtfully. "He's facing a long prison sentence. If we can offer him a way to help himself, maybe by leading the sheriff to a bigger prize like Collins, he might cooperate. And besides, we have something the police don't."

"What's that?" Scotty asked.

"We found his projector. There might be something in that cave he doesn't want the police to find. A little leverage can't hurt."

The trip back to town was made in a thoughtful silence. They found the sheriff at the small county jail, a brick building next to the courthouse. He was surprised to see them but, after Rick's earnest explanation, he grudgingly agreed to let them have five minutes with the prisoner. "Don't promise him anything I can't deliver," he warned. "But if you can get a lead on Collins, I'm all ears."

Miller, the ice-cream man, sat on a cot in a small, clean cell. He looked up as they approached, his face a mixture of resentment and fear. His rumpled white uniform was smudged with dirt from the cave floor.

"What do you kids want?" he mumbled, not meeting their eyes. "Haven't you done enough?"

"We want to help you, Mr. Miller," Rick began, his voice even and calm.

Miller let out a short, bitter laugh. "Help me? You got me put in here. Some help."

"You were going to get caught eventually," Scotty pointed out. "We just made it sooner rather than later. The sheriff is looking at a long list of charges. Fraud, conspiracy, trespassing on state property."

"Jethro is the one you want," Miller said sullenly. "It was all his idea. The ghost, the searching. I was just the hired help."

"We know," Rick said. "And that's why we're here. Collins is gone. He ran out on you, left you to take the fall. If you help us find him, the sheriff might be inclined to tell the judge you cooperated."

Miller was silent for a moment, considering. "I don't know where he went. He had plans in case things went sour, but he never told me what they were. Said it was better if I didn't know."

"Then tell us what you were looking for," Rick pressed. "What is this treasure? If we know what it is, we might be able to figure out where he'd go to get it."

Miller stared at the concrete floor between his worn shoes. His shoulders sagged. Rick could see the man wasn't a hardened criminal, just someone who had made a series of very bad choices. He was in over his head, and now he was drowning.

"Look, Mr. Miller," Rick tried again, his tone patient. "We know you're not the brains of this operation. But right now, you're the only one the sheriff has. All the charges that could be filed against Collins are going to stick to you instead. Unless you give them a reason to go after him harder than they're going after you."

"He'll never tell the judge I helped," Miller grumbled. "He'll take all the credit."

"Maybe," Scotty chimed in, leaning against the bars. "But the sheriff is an honest man. He told us so himself. If you help catch Collins, he'll see to it that the prosecutor knows you cooperated. It's your only chance."

Miller looked from one boy to the other, a flicker of hope warring with his ingrained mistrust. "What do you want to know? Like I said, I don't know where he's gone."

"Tell us what you were looking for," Rick repeated. "What is it about the Spindrift Mine? Is there Confederate gold?"

Miller actually snorted, a brief, humorless sound. "Gold? No. Nothing so simple. It was never about gold." He hesitated, chewing on his lower lip. "Collins is a student of local history. The real stuff, not the stories they put in the tourist brochures. He spends all his time in the county records office, looking at old deeds, old surveys, old wills."

"For his real-estate business," Scotty guessed.

"That's how it started," Miller affirmed. "But he got obsessed. He found references to a man, a Confederate officer named Major Beaugard. He wasn't a soldier, not really. He was a paymaster. And a spymaster. He operated out of this area during the war."

Rick leaned closer to the bars. "And he hid something at the mine?"

"Not at the mine. Near it. That was the whole point of the Blue Ghost. Jethro figured the local legends about the mine were a cover. The stories were meant to keep people away from the whole area. He thought Beaugard himself might have started them. The ghost was just our way of keeping people away while we searched."

"Searched for what?" Rick pressed.

Miller finally looked up, his eyes meeting Rick's. The fear was still there, but now it was mixed with a strange kind of excitement, the pride of a man sharing a secret he has held for too long.

"A journal," he said, his voice dropping to a near whisper. "Beaugard's personal journal. According to the letters Jethro found, the journal contains a complete record of Beaugard's activities. But the important part, the part Jethro wants, is a ledger."

"A ledger of what? Payments?"

"Bribes," Miller corrected. "Beaugard wasn't just paying his own spies. He was buying information. He was paying off Union sympathizers, prominent citizens, people who were publicly supporting the North but selling secrets to the South on the side. The ledger has all their names, what they did, and how much they were paid."

Rick and Scotty exchanged a look. The implications were staggering. "But that was over a hundred years ago," Scotty said. "Who would care now?"

"Their families," Miller answered. "Jethro traced the family lines. Three of the names on that list belong to families that are still the wealthiest and most powerful in this part of Virginia. Their fortunes were founded on land and businesses they held through the war, protected by their reputations as staunch Unionists. What do you think would happen if a journal came to light that proved their great-grandfathers were traitors, selling out their own side for money?"

Rick felt a chill. "Blackmail."

"Jethro called it leverage," Miller said bitterly. "He's a real-estate man. He figured he could use the journal to pressure those families into certain business deals. Sell him land for pennies on the dollar. Give him controlling interest in their companies. With that journal, he could own this county."

"And the ghost wagon Belsely saw?" Rick asked. "The men searching the ground?"

"We were looking," Miller admitted. "Jethro had narrowed the search area down to the fields on top of the mine hill. He had a theory the journal was buried in a small, lead-lined box. We were using a new kind of metal detector he'd bought. We'd go out late at night. The 'ghost wagon' was just a garden cart we used to carry the equipment, disguised to look spooky from a distance, just in case anyone saw us."

"So you don't know the exact spot," Scotty stated.

"No. Jethro had a final clue, he said. A piece of the puzzle he'd figured out just this week. He was excited, said we were close. He never told me what it was. Said he'd know the place when he saw it."

A guard appeared at the end of the hall. "Time's up, boys."

"One more thing," Rick said urgently, his mind racing. "Did he ever mention any landmarks? Anything at all? A name, a phrase from a song, anything."

Miller thought for a second, his brow furrowed. "There was something. A line he kept repeating to himself the last few days. From some old poem or story, I think. He said it was the key."

"What was it?"

"He said, 'The answer is where the silent sentinel watches the fallen eagle'." Miller shook his head. "It's nonsense. Just old stories. But he was convinced it was a map."

"Thank you, Mr. Miller," Rick said, just as the guard arrived to escort them away. "You've been a big help."

"Just get him," Miller called after them. "Just make sure Jethro Collins doesn't get away with it."

The boys walked out of the jail and into the bright afternoon sun, blinking. The world seemed too normal, too quiet for the kind of high-stakes drama that was unfolding.

"The silent sentinel watches the fallen eagle," Scotty repeated, tasting the words. "Sounds like something out of a bad adventure novel."

"It's not a novel to Collins," Rick said grimly. "It's a treasure map. And he's got a big head start. We need to figure out what it means, and fast."

"Where do we start? The library?"

"That's the logical place," Rick agreed. "Collins was a history nut who hung around the records office. The clue is probably tied to local history. Let's go."

The town library was a small, stone building that smelled of old paper and floor polish. The librarian, a kindly woman with white hair and glasses, knew Rick and Scotty from their previous visits and was happy to help.

"Civil War history?" she said, leading them to a dusty corner. "We have a wonderful local collection. Diaries, old newspapers, maps. Is it for a school project?"

"Something like that," Rick said evasively.

They spread their materials out on a heavy oak table. For an hour, they pored over brittle maps and books filled with fine print. They found dozens of references to eagles, from a tavern called The Eagle's Perch to a Union cavalry unit nicknamed the "Soaring Eagles." Nothing seemed to fit.

"This is getting us nowhere," Scotty said in frustration, pushing a stack of books away. "Fallen eagle could mean anything. A dead bird, a defeat in battle, a statue that fell over."

"Wait a minute," Rick said, his finger tracing a line on an old military survey map from 1863. "Look at this." He pointed to a high ridge a few miles north of town. "A failed assault," Scotty read. "The eagle has fallen. That has to be it! It was a union regiment, too. An eagle falling on its own crest."

"Exactly," Rick said, his excitement growing. "Collins would know this. It's a famous local story. So if Eagle's Crest is the fallen eagle, what's the silent sentinel?"

"A statue?" Scotty suggested. "A monument to the soldiers who died there?"

"Maybe. But Miller said Collins spent his time with deeds and surveys. What's important to a surveyor?"

"That's it," Rick whispered. "A survey marker. They're usually stone pillars, obelisks. They don't speak, they just stand there, watching. A silent sentinel."

"Watching the fallen eagle," Scotty finished, his eyes wide. "Rick, you're a genius."

"Collins is the genius," Rick corrected, already folding the map. "He put it all together from historical scraps. The spot isn't on the mine property at all. It's on state forest land, but it overlooks the whole area. It's the perfect hiding place."

They ran out of the library, calling a hasty thank you to the bewildered librarian. They found the sheriff just getting into his car.

"Sheriff!" Rick called, running up to the window. "We know where Collins is going!"

He quickly explained their theory, pointing out the location on the map. The sheriff listened intently, his expression grim.

"That makes a terrifying amount of sense," the sheriff said when Rick had finished. "That marker is way up in the hills. It'll take me at least an hour to get a team organized and drive up the logging road. He'll be long gone by then." He looked at the boys. "I'm ordering you two to stay out of this. Collins is a desperate man. He found a gun in the cave, and we don't know if he has another one. This is police business now."

"But he'll get away!" Scotty protested.

"He won't get far," the sheriff promised. "Now go home. That's an order."

He sped off, leaving the boys in a cloud of dust.

Rick and Scotty looked at each other. "He's right, you know," Scotty said. "It's dangerous."

"I know," Rick said. "And he's also right that Collins will be gone by the time the deputies get there. He'll have the journal and disappear. Those families will be living under his thumb forever." He looked toward the hills, his jaw set. "We can't let that happen."
